The process of obtaining informed consent, conducting eligibility screening, receiving recruits for respondent-driven sampling (RDS), providing counseling and testing, and returning results (if applicable) must be carefully managed to ensure ethical and procedural compliance. 2. Once staff members are trained in their respective roles, a practice session simulating survey activities should be conducted. This session should use a mock survey within a population similar to the intended target population to familiarize staff with the survey event process. 3. The practice session should adhere to the prescribed flow of events and aim to be as realistic as possible. After the exercise, the trainer should evaluate staff knowledge of their roles and assess their performance in carrying out the activities. 4. Survey implementation and quality assurance are critical components of the process, as are data analysis and the effective use of findings. 5. During survey preparation, stakeholders must be identified, and planning considerations should address the specific requirements of a biobehavioral survey. Ethical considerations must be integrated into both the planning and execution phases. 6. Formative assessments should be conducted to inform the development of questionnaires and the selection of biomarkers. Instruments for biological data collection must be prepared in advance. 7. Eligibility criteria for participation should be clearly defined, and a sampling strategy must be developed. This includes determining the required sample size and estimating the population size using appropriate methods. 8. Supplemental studies may be considered, and robust data management systems should be established. Staff selection and training are essential, and standard operating procedures (SOPs) must be developed and followed. 9. Nonprobability sampling methods, such as convenience sampling, purposive sampling, quota sampling, and chain-referral sampling (e.g., snowball sampling), are often employed when probability-based designs are not feasible due to cost, complexity, or inaccessibility of the target population. 10. Convenience sampling involves recruiting participants based on ease of access, such as individuals frequenting community-based organizations or drop-in centers. While this method facilitates sampling, it does not ensure representativeness. 11. Purposive sampling targets specific subsets of a population, such as men who have sex with men (MSM) who are married to women or HIV-infected individuals. Recruitment strategies may include peer referral or sampling at antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinics. 12. Quota sampling aims to include a predetermined number of participants with specific characteristics to ensure diversity or representativeness. For example, investigators may sample a set number of people who inject drugs (PWID) with known and unknown HIV statuses. 13. Snowball sampling begins with purposively selected participants who then assist in recruiting others. This method is particularly useful when members of the target population are interconnected. 14. Recruitment strategies may involve engaging participants at commercial venues, public spaces, service providers, community-based organizations, or through online platforms. Investigators should consider the unique operational requirements of each method. 15. Sampling at venues such as bars, clubs, parks, or brothels may be effective if the target population frequents these locations. Permission from venue owners may be required, and sampling from diverse locations can reduce bias. 16. Service providers and community-based organizations can help identify and recruit participants. Direct sampling at service delivery sites is preferred for efficiency, but alternative methods, such as distributing vouchers or flyers, may also be used. 17. Internet-based recruitment can involve placing survey links on relevant websites or using email invitations. Investigators must ensure participant anonymity and protect personal identifiers, such as IP addresses. 18. Preparation for sampling includes contacting gatekeepers, explaining survey objectives, and setting expectations for survey activities. Private areas for interviews and specimen collection should be identified, and staff must be trained in participant protections and confidentiality. 19. During enrollment and data collection, measures should be taken to ensure data quality and minimize errors. Security considerations for both staff and participants are also important. 20. Survey staff should adhere to the survey protocol and flow chart of activities, whether data collection occurs at a venue, in a mobile unit, or at a fixed survey office. Sampling may need to occur during times when the target population is most accessible. 21. Monitoring survey progress involves documenting the number of individuals screened, eligible, consenting, and participating in specimen collection. Reasons for refusal should also be recorded, and the use of vouchers or coupons should be tracked. 22. Adherence to SOPs is essential for both probability and nonprobability sampling methods. Survey progress and sample composition should be monitored to assess biases and data quality. 23. Conventional cluster sampling (CCS) is appropriate when the target population is associated with fixed clusters, such as brothels, prisons, or treatment facilities. Preparations include mapping cluster locations, creating participant lists, and ensuring confidentiality and anonymity. 24. During the planning phase, logistical considerations for participant sampling at each cluster location must be addressed. This includes contacting gatekeepers, arranging private areas for data collection, and training staff on survey procedures.
